question.prompt: In acute triangle \(ABC\) the bisector of \(\angle A\) meets side \(BC\) at \(D.\) The circle with center \(B\) and radius \(BD\) intersects side \(AB\) at \(M;\) and the circle with center \(C\) and radius \(CD\) intersects side \(AC\) at \(N.\) Then it is always true that

solutions.explanation:
The circles give \(BM=BD\) and \(CN=CD\). To relate \(MN\) to \(BC\), compare the fractions of \(AB\) and \(AC\) that these equal lengths remove.

Since \(AD\) is the internal angle bisector, the angle bisector theorem gives
\[
\frac{BD}{CD}=\frac{AB}{AC}.
\]
All these lengths are positive, so we may rearrange this as
\[
\frac{BD}{AB}=\frac{CD}{AC}=k,
\]
where \(k>0\). Adding \(BD=kAB\) and \(CD=kAC\) yields
\[
k=\frac{BC}{AB+AC}<1
\]
by the triangle inequality. Thus \(BM=kAB<AB\) and \(CN=kAC<AC\), confirming that \(M\) and \(N\) are strictly inside their respective sides.

Subtracting these portions leaves the same fraction of each side:
\[
\frac{AM}{AB}=1-\frac{BM}{AB}=1-k,
\qquad
\frac{AN}{AC}=1-\frac{CN}{AC}=1-k.
\]
Therefore \(\triangle AMN\) and \(\triangle ABC\) have two corresponding sides in proportion and the same included angle at \(A\). By SAS similarity, they are similar, giving \(\angle AMN=\angle ABC\). These are corresponding angles along transversal \(AB\), so \(MN\parallel BC\). The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Angle bisector ratios and similarity
